articles.content: Reporting entities, as well as their Board members, officers and employees, are prohibited from disclosing or insinuating to anyone that a suspicious transaction report or other relevant information is submitted or intended to be submitted to the Commission, or that the Commission is inquiring about customers or auditing their operations or accounts.

articles.title: Immunity
articles.content: Within the scope of their work, the Chairman, members, staff and delegates of the Commission, shall enjoy immunity. Thus, they may not be prosecuted or sued, neither collectively nor individually, for any civil or criminal liability related to the performance of their duties. The parties referred to in Articles 4 and 5 above and their staff shall also enjoy the same immunity when they report in good faith to the Commission the details of operations they suspect to be related to money laundering or terrorist financing.

articles.title: Penalties for Non-Compliance
articles.content: Any party that violates the provisions of Articles 4, 5, 7, 10, and 11 of this Law shall be punishable by imprisonment for a period of two months to one year and by a fine not exceeding one hundred million Lebanese pounds, or by either penalties. The Commission may address a warning to the parties who are in violation of the provisions of the regulations issued for the purpose of implementing this Law. The Higher Banking Commission may impose on the parties that were referred to it a fine for non-compliance, provided this fine does not exceed two hundred times the official minimum wage.

articles.title: Confiscation
articles.content: The movable or immovable assets that are proved, by a final Court ruling, to be related to, or derived from, a money-laundering or terrorist financing offence, shall be confiscated to the benefit of the State, unless the owners of the said assets prove in a Court of Law their legal rights thereupon. The confiscated assets may be shared with other countries, whenever the confiscation results directly from coordinated investigations or cooperation between the concerned Lebanese authorities and the concerned foreign body(ies).

articles.title: Entry into Force
articles.content: This Law shall enter into force upon its publication in the Official Gazette. Beirut, November 24, 2015. Promulgated by the Council of Ministers. The President of the Council of Ministers. Signed: Tammam Salam.

additional_laws.title_en: Law No. 81 of October 10, 2018 Relating to Electronic Transactions and Personal Data
additional_laws.title_ar: القانون رقم 81 تاريخ 10 أكتوبر 2018 المتعلق بالمعاملات الإلكترونية والبيانات الشخصية
additional_laws.source: SMEX – Social Media Exchange (Official Gazette English Translation)
additional_laws.historical_context: Lebanon's Electronic Transactions and Personal Data Law was enacted on October 10, 2018 (effective three months after publication). It was based on a draft law issued by Decree No. 9341 of November 17, 2012. The law establishes the legal framework for electronic writing and signatures, electronic commerce and contracts, electronic banking and financial services, electronic government, and personal data protection. It created COLIBAC (Lebanese Accreditation Council) as the body responsible for accrediting electronic authentication service providers.

articles.title: Definitions
articles.content: For the purposes of the present law: Writing: The process of writing or recording letters, numbers, characters or symbols, provided that they are legible and comprehensible, regardless of the format used. Electronic Document: An ordinary or official document issued in an electronic form pursuant to Article 8 herein. Signature: The signature required to complete a legal process in order to identify the party thereto and confirm their consent. Service Provider: A public or private law enforcement officer who issues the certificates of authentication. Electronic Commerce: An activity whereby a person provides or remotely offers goods and services to another person. Bank Card: An instrument issued by a bank allowing its holder to withdraw cash money or perform electronic payments or any other banking or financial services. Electronic Money: Electronic monetary units stored in electronic form. Network Service Provider: A business or organization that enables the user to access an electronic communication network. Data Host: A system used to store third-party information of any type and make it accessible to the public. Traffic Data: Any data relating to a communication by means of a computer connected to the network, generated by a computer system and indicating the communication's origin, destination, route, format, intent, time, date, size, duration. Domain Name: The system used to translate the alphanumeric domain name of a website into an Internet Protocol number. Personal Data: Any information that helps to directly or indirectly identify a natural person. Processing of Personal Data: Any action or set of actions performed on the data regardless of the medium used, including data collection, recording, organization, storage, adaptation, modification, extraction, reading, use, transmission, copy, dissemination, deletion, destruction or otherwise disposing of it.

articles.title: Principle
articles.content: The information technology is at the service of the people, provided that it does not prejudice their individual identity, rights, private life, or individual or public freedoms.

articles.title: Legal Effect of Electronic Writing
articles.content: Electronic writings and signatures shall have the same legal effect as the writings and signatures made on paper or any other medium, provided that the person producing them is identifiable and that they are organized and stored in a way that preserves their safety. Any electronic writing that does not meet the criteria above shall be considered as introduction of written evidence.

articles.title: Electronic Documents as Evidence
articles.content: The electronic document shall be accepted as evidence and is deemed to have the same significance and power of proof as the written paper-based document, provided that it is possible to identify the person issuing the document and that the latter is organized and stored in a way that ensures its integrity.

articles.title: Official Electronic Documents
articles.content: Official electronic documents do not produce any legal effects unless they are organized and governed by virtue of a decree issued by the Council of Ministers upon a proposal by the Minister of Justice.

articles.title: Electronic Signature
articles.content: The electronic signature is issued through the use of a safe medium that identifies the signatory and provides a guarantee that the signature corresponds to the legal process in question. If the signature is linked to the protection measures authenticated by the authorized authentication service provider, it shall be presumed to have satisfied the criteria set forth in this Article, unless proven otherwise.

articles.title: Freedom of Electronic Writing
articles.content: Electronic writing is a free act, and no person shall be bound to resort to protection means unless otherwise stipulated by the law.

articles.title: Protection Measures
articles.content: The protection measures are used in electronic writings and signatures to make them more reliable. The protection measures help perform several functions, such as verifying the identity of the document organizer, assigning a correct date to the document, and/or ensuring its storage and the integrity of its content. Any and all functions above are provided by one or more authentication service provider who shall, upon performance of said functions, deliver a certificate of authentication to the concerned person.

articles.title: COLIBAC Accreditation
articles.content: COLIBAC accredits those authentication service providers who issue certificates to electronic writings and signature provided they meet the requirements outlined in Articles (7) and (9) above. COLIBAC decisions regarding the implementation of the present Law may be challenged before the State Council.

articles.title: Freedom of Electronic Commerce
articles.content: Electronic commerce shall be free to the extent permissible by law. All matters related to e-commerce and not mentioned in the present law shall be governed by the applicable laws, particularly the Code of Commerce, the Code of Obligations and Contracts, the Civil Procedure Law and the Consumer Protection Law.

articles.title: Disclosure Obligations in E-Commerce
articles.content: All persons practicing e-commerce as a business must ensure to the persons they deal with an easy and direct access to the following information at all times: 1- For natural persons, their first name, last name and place of residence. 2- For legal entities, their name, the name of their legal representative, their headquarters and their commercial address. 3- The detailed address, email, website, and telephone number. 4- Number and Place of registration at the Commercial Registry and the competent tax department. 5- Their professional capacity and the professional rules governing their business. 6- A detailed statement outlining the price and any payable tax, fee or expenses.

articles.title: Prohibition on Spam
articles.content: Promotional ads that are accessible online through any electronic device should contain a reference to indicate that the material is a promotional ad. It is forbidden to communicate unsolicited marketing and advertising emails (SPAM) using a real person's name and address, unless that person has consented to such type of advertising, except for cases where the sender of the unsolicited advertisement has legally obtained the client's address through a previous engagement with them. Every promotional or marketing email should contain a reference to an email which the recipient can reply to in order to request that they stop receiving such emails permanently and free of charge.

articles.title: Electronic Contract Formation Requirements
articles.content: Any person who offers, as part of their business, goods or services by electronic means shall include the following in their offerings: 1- Steps to follow to sign the contract electronically. 2- The contract terms and conditions in a form that can be saved and duplicated. 3- Technical features that allow the addressee to double check the electronic contract for errors and correct the same before submitting the final approval. 4- To which extent the offeror undertakes to store the digital traces. 5- The contract official language.

articles.title: Contract Formation in Civil and Commercial Matters
articles.content: The acceptance of the electronic means to be used in civil or commercial contracts shall not be considered sufficient to originate the contract. The addressee may re-examine the parties' contractual obligations before confirming their will to proceed with the contract. When bargains in civil and commercial contracts are made electronically, the contract shall only be originated when the offeror receives the addressee's consent. An electronic communication is taken to be dispatched when it enters the first information system outside the sender's control.

articles.title: Electronic Payment Definition
articles.content: An electronic payment or money transfer is an operation carried out, partly or entirely, by electronic means. In order to perform such operation, the client authorizes the bank, the financial institution or any institution legally authorized or licensed by Banque du Liban to perform an electronic payment operation.

articles.title: Client Consent for Electronic Payments
articles.content: The client shall give his prior written consent to the conditions governing electronic payments, transfers or cancellation thereof, provided that such conditions are clear, explicit and compliant with Banque du Liban regulations, include the rights and obligations relating to electronic banking services and determine the fees, expenses, commissions and taxes, if any.

articles.title: Client Liability for Unauthorized Transactions
articles.content: Except in cases of serious error, gross negligence or bad faith, the client shall not be responsible for any electronic payment or transfer transaction made to their account provided that they promptly notify in writing the institutions referred to in Article (41) above within 90 days of the date of the transaction resulting from: A third party might have accessed their account illegally; A third party might have known their account personal identification number (PIN); The client knows that an operation was performed through their account either without their consent or knowledge, or by mistake, or illegally.

articles.title: Written Form for Payment Orders
articles.content: The orders to perform electronic payments and transfers shall be made in writing and shall be manually or electronically signed, under penalty of nullity. If orders are electronically signed, the signature shall be authenticated in accordance with the rules issued by the Banque du Liban.

additional_laws.title_en: Law No. 65/2017 on the Punishment of Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment (Anti-Torture Law)
additional_laws.title_ar: القانون رقم 65/2017 المتعلق بقمع التعذيب وغيره من ضروب المعاملة أو العقوبة القاسية أو اللاإنسانية أو المهينة
additional_laws.source: National Human Rights Commission Lebanon (NHRCLB); CLDH Lebanon
additional_laws.historical_context: Law No. 65/2017 was adopted by the Lebanese Parliament on September 19, 2017, marking the first time that Lebanese legislation explicitly criminalized torture. Lebanon had ratified the UN Convention against Torture (CAT) in 2000 and its Optional Protocol (OPCAT) in 2008. The law amended Articles 401 and 185 of the Penal Code and Article 10 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. However, the law has been criticized by international human rights bodies for having an overly narrow definition of torture, setting a statute of limitations, imposing insufficiently grave penalties, and failing to explicitly require torture cases to be heard in civilian (rather than military) courts.

articles.title: Incriminating Torture – Amendment to Article 401 of the Penal Code
articles.content: Article 401 of the Criminal Code shall be amended to read as follows: a- 'Torture under the present Law shall include any act inflicted by or at the instigation of or with the consent or acquiescence of a public official or other person acting in an official capacity during the preliminary survey and investigations, judicial investigation, trials and punishments resulting in severe pain or suffering, whether physical or mental, intentionally inflicted on a person for the purposes below: obtaining from him/her or a third person information or a confession; punishing him/her for an act he/she or a third person has committed or is suspected of having committed; intimidating or coercing him/her or a third person into engaging in an act or refraining therefrom; inflicting such pain or suffering for any reason based on discrimination of any kind. The definition above does not include pain or suffering arising only from, inherent in or incidental to, lawful sanctions.' b- Anyone who practices torture shall be liable to imprisonment as follows: One to three years in prison for cases that do not result in physical or psychological harm; Three to seven years if it leads to temporary disability, harm, or physical or psychological impairment; Five to ten years if the harm is permanent; Ten to twenty years if it leads to death. c- Court shall determine the measure of rehabilitating the victims of torture in addition to personal compensation.

articles.title: Special Provisions on Illegal Orders – Amendment to Article 185 of the Penal Code
articles.content: The following two paragraphs shall be added to Article 185 of the Criminal Code: 'Whoever is prosecuted for any of the crimes under Article 401 of the present law, shall, on no account, allege necessity, national security requirements, orders of the supreme hierarchy or any other pretext.' 'The orders of torture issued by a public officer, of any rank, agency of authority, shall not be considered legitimate orders in any case.'

articles.title: Statute of Limitations – Amendment to Code of Criminal Procedure
articles.content: By virtue of this Article and Article 10 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the crime of torture is subjected to the ten-year statute of limitation (felony prescription period), which starts to run upon the victim's release from custody or detention.

articles.title: Inadmissibility of Evidence Obtained Under Duress
articles.content: Any evidence or confession obtained through the use of torture, coercion or any form of duress shall be inadmissible in any judicial proceedings. Courts are required to exclude such evidence and to refer the matter for investigation of the alleged torture.

articles.title: Obligations of Judicial Authorities
articles.content: Judicial authorities are required to promptly and impartially consider complaints of torture. In accordance with Article 13 of the UN Convention against Torture, the bill proposes a set of provisions aimed at ensuring the effectiveness of complaints submitted by all those who claim to be subjected to torture and that the competent judicial authorities shall consider such complaints promptly and impartially. Victims of torture are entitled to file complaints and to have access to full reparation including rehabilitation and compensation independent of criminal proceedings.

articles.title: Entry into Force
articles.content: This Law shall enter into force upon its publication in the Official Gazette.

additional_laws.title_en: Social Security Law (Decree-Law No. 13955 of September 26, 1963)
additional_laws.title_ar: قانون الضمان الاجتماعي (المرسوم الاشتراعي رقم 13955 تاريخ 26 سبتمبر 1963)
additional_laws.historical_context: Lebanon's Social Security Law was promulgated by Decree-Law No. 13955 of September 26, 1963, establishing the National Social Security Fund (NSSF or CNSS in French). The law created a comprehensive social protection system covering four branches: sickness-maternity insurance, labor accidents and occupational diseases insurance, family allowances, and end-of-service indemnity. The Fund is governed by a Board of Directors with tripartite representation from the state, employers, and workers. The law has been amended numerous times, most significantly by Laws No. 9/74 (1974), 12/78 (1978), 15/69 (1969), and 27/88 (1988).

articles.title: Establishment of National Social Security Fund
articles.content: 1 - A Social Security National Fund shall be set up, referred to in the present law by the term 'Fund'. Its terms of reference shall be the management of the whole of the social security system including its various branches. 2 - The Fund shall be an autonomous institution of a social character, governed by the provisions of the present law. It shall be vested with corporate personality as well as with financial and managerial autonomy. Its registered office shall be in Beirut, and it shall be authorised to set up regional and local offices. 3 - Within the limitations set out in Article 3 of the present law, the Fund shall be subject to: A - The guardianship of the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs, through a Government Commissioner; B - The prior guardianship of the Council of Ministers; C - The subsequent control of the Audit Office, to the exclusion of any prior control. 4 - The machinery of the Fund shall be made up of the Board of Directors, the Technical Commission and the Secretariat. 5 - The Fund shall be subject to the control of neither the Civil Service Council nor of Central Inspectorate.

articles.title: Board of Directors Composition
articles.content: The Board of Directors shall be composed of the following delegates: A - Six delegates representing the State; B - Ten delegates from professional organisations most representative of employers; C - Ten delegates from professional organisations most representative of wage-earners and salary-earners (workmen and employees); D - Delegates from agricultural organisations. Decisions shall be taken by the Board of Directors and by the Office Committee by absolute majority vote. Each delegate shall have one vote, and in case of a tie, the President's vote shall have casting power. The majority voting for the decision in the Board of Directors, must consist of the absolute majority of each group of representatives.

articles.title: Powers of the Board of Directors
articles.content: Powers of the Fund's Board of Directors shall notably be the following: 1 - Without prejudice to any decree from the Council of Ministers: organization and nomination of the Financial Commission; vesting the Director General with authority to acquire real estate for internal operation of the Fund. 2 - Activities which require the approval of the guardianship Authority: issuance of Internal Regulations; producing the administrative budget; closing the accounts; setting priorities for social investments; laying down the ground-work for creation of new local and regional offices. 3 - Activities within the competence of the Office Committee: decisions which need not be submitted to the Council of Ministers; decisions related to administrative or technical matters.

articles.title: Director General
articles.content: 1 - The Fund's Secretariat shall be headed by a Director General. The latter shall be appointed by decree emanating from the Council of Ministers, on the proposal of the Minister of Labour and Social Affairs after approval of the Board of Directors. 2 - Only a university graduate holding a recognised degree, and duly qualified in social, administrative or financial matters and with some banking and insurance experience may be appointed. 3 - The Director General shall be held for the implementation of the resolutions adopted by the Board, as well as for the management of the Fund's Secretariat.

articles.title: Branches of Social Security
articles.content: Social Security shall comprise the following branches: A - Sickness-maternity insurance. B - Labour accidents-occupational diseases insurance. C - Family allowance regime. D - End-of-service indemnity regime. It shall be applied in three stages.

articles.title: Scope of Application
articles.content: Shall be subject to the provisions of the present law, as from the first stage, on condition that activity is exercised on the Lebanese territory: A - Lebanese wage-earners and salary-earners, permanent, temporary, apprentices, seasonal, and trainees, working for the account of one or several Lebanese or foreign employers, whatever may be the duration, kind, nature, form or validity of the contracts binding them to their employer; B - Lebanese wage-earners and salary-earners unattached to any particular employer, and who work in the maritime sector, ports, enterprises, building, transport and unloading; C - Members of the teaching staff in Lebanese higher education establishments; D - Lebanese nationals who work for the account of the State or Municipalities or any other Administration, Public Establishment or Autonomous Office.

additional_laws.title_en: Law on Collective Labor Contracts, Mediation and Arbitration (Decree-Law No. 17386/1964)
additional_laws.title_ar: قانون عقود العمل الجماعية والتوفيق والتحكيم (المرسوم الاشتراعي رقم 17386/1964)
additional_laws.source: MONDAQ – Lebanon Labour and Employment Comparative Guide; UNHCR Lebanon Labour Sector Report
additional_laws.historical_context: Lebanon's Collective Labor Contracts, Mediation and Arbitration Law was enacted by Decree-Law No. 17386 in 1964, providing the legal framework for collective bargaining alongside the individual employment framework under the 1946 Labour Law. The law establishes mechanisms for negotiating, registering, and enforcing collective employment contracts between trade unions and employers, and provides for mediation and arbitration as dispute resolution mechanisms for collective labor disputes.

articles.title: Definition of Collective Employment Contract
articles.content: A collective employment contract is an instrument governing employment terms that is concluded between a party representing one or more workers' trade union and another party, who may be an individual employer, a group of employers, a representative of one or more professional body or union of employers. Collective employment contracts are designed to regulate the conditions of employment stipulated in individual contracts between the parties bound by the agreement.

articles.title: Representative Authority
articles.content: The employee representative must be vested with the authorisation of at least 60% of the relevant employees in order to negotiate a collective agreement.

articles.title: Written Form and Registration
articles.content: The collective agreement shall be executed in writing and becomes binding upon the earlier of: publication in the Official Gazette by the Ministry of Labour; or one month after its registration at the Ministry of Labour.

articles.title: Adhesion to Existing Agreements
articles.content: Any trade union, professional body or employer that is not a party to the collective agreement can unilaterally decide to join the collective agreement without the consent of the initial signatories, by virtue of a written request submitted to the Ministry of Labour.

articles.title: Mediation for Collective Disputes
articles.content: The Collective Agreements Law encourages alternative dispute resolution and provides for mediation as a first attempt to settle collective labor disputes. A dispute is considered a collective labour dispute where a party to the dispute is a group of employees and the dispute pertains to a collective interest.

articles.title: Arbitration Commission
articles.content: If the mediation process is wholly or partially unsuccessful, the parties may resort to arbitration before the Arbitration Commission for the Resolution of Collective Labour Disputes, established pursuant to this Law. The commission consists of representatives of employees, employers and the Ministry of Labour. The commission's decision is final.

articles.title: Special Committee Arbitration
articles.content: The parties can agree in a collective agreement or private contract to resolve the dispute before a special committee other than the Arbitration Commission for the Resolution of Collective Labour Disputes (except in certain cases where it is mandatory to refer the matter to the commission). The decision of the special committee may be subject to appeal to the arbitration commission, which must issue its decision within one month of the date of the first session – a timeframe which the arbitration commission can extend by two weeks where necessary.

additional_laws.title_en: Rent Laws: Law No. 159/1992 (New Leases), Law No. 160/1992 (Old Leases), and Law No. 9/2014 (New Tenancy Law)
additional_laws.title_ar: قوانين الإيجار: القانون رقم 159/1992 (الإيجارات الجديدة) والقانون رقم 160/1992 (الإيجارات القديمة) والقانون رقم 9/2014 (قانون الإيجار الجديد)
additional_laws.source: Monthly Magazine Lebanon; Arab Land Initiative / UN-Habitat; Academia.edu
additional_laws.historical_context: Post-civil war Lebanon enacted two complementary rent laws in July 1992. Law No. 159 of July 22, 1992 introduced 'freedom of contract' for new leases (signed after July 22, 1992), replacing the previous mandatory renewal system. Law No. 160 of July 22, 1992 governed old leases (signed before July 23, 1992), providing a phased rent increase framework and limited landlord rights to reclaim property. Law No. 160 was extended 12 times over the following decades. In April 2014, the New Tenancy Law (Law 9/2014) was enacted to gradually liberalize all old rent contracts through a 9-year transition period with annual rent increases tied to property market values, supported by a rent assistance fund for vulnerable tenants.

articles.title: Freedom of Contract for New Leases (Art. 1 of Law 159/1992)
articles.content: The leases of both residential and non-residential property shall be subject to freedom of contract and to the will of the contracting parties in all that does not contradict the following binding provisions: First: if the lease period specified in the lease agreement is less than three years, the lease shall still be considered for a period of three years. Second: excluded from the previous provision are all the seasonal leases concerned with summer and winter vacation premises and the leases of property granted by employers to employees with or without a charge. Third: if the period of the lease agreement, whether of built property or land, exceeds three years, the property may not be passed to a third party unless it is first registered in the cadastral registry.

articles.title: Rental Increases for Old Leases (Art. 1 of Law 160/1992)
articles.content: For lease agreements signed prior to July 22, 1990: Raising rental fees by half the successive wage hikes affecting the first salary bracket and determined by the decrees pertaining to the cost of living and the pay of employees as of July 1, 1987 and successively upon every future rise. Law No. 160 also postulated doubling the rental fees according to the year of the lease agreement in favor of landlords and granted them the right to regain their property should they or a member of their family need the dwelling for personal use, provided that they pay the tenant a compensation estimated by the courts of not less than 25% and not more than 50% of the property value.

articles.title: Scope of New Tenancy Law
articles.content: Subject to the provisions of this law are all the lease agreements regarding built property signed prior to July 23, 1992 with the exception of: 1) the leases of agricultural land and the facilities on it; 2) the seasonal leases concerned with summer and winter vacation premises; 3) the leases of property granted by employers to employees for accommodation; 4) the leases on villas fulfilling certain specifications established by the law; 5) the leases on the state and the municipal public properties.

articles.title: Transition Period and Extension
articles.content: The newly approved Rent Act extended lease agreements by nine years starting on the date of its entry into force and permitted a further extension of three additional years upon expiry of the first nine year period at the same rental rates paid during the ninth year.

articles.title: Rent Increase Formula
articles.content: During the period of the lease agreement extension, rents increase by a gradual percentage – a percentage of the dwelling's rental value in the free market – that is either agreed upon by the mutual consent of the contracting parties or determined, in case of disagreement, by two court experts. The free market rental value is determined on the basis of 5% of the sale value of the rented dwelling in its current condition if vacant. Increases proceed: by 15% of the difference between old and new rental value for each of the first four extended years; by 20% of the difference for each of the fifth and sixth years, until fees reach the full rental value; after this time, between the seventh and the ninth extended years, the property will be rented at free market prices.

articles.title: Eviction in Case of Necessity
articles.content: If the landlord wishes to recover his property for family-related reasons during the first year of the nine-year extension period, he shall pay the tenant a compensation equivalent to the rental cost sustained over four years on the basis of the specified free market rental value. However, if he plans to evict the tenant in the first year in order to demolish the building and replace it with a newer one, he shall pay the tenant a compensation amounting to the annual rents paid within six years.

articles.title: Rent Assistance Fund
articles.content: A rent assistance fund is established to support needy tenants unable to afford the rent increases. The fund excludes foreign tenants and Lebanese tenants who rent property deemed luxurious. The implementation of the provisions related to the rent increases and the applications submitted to the fund for assistance will be entrusted to a judicial committee consisting of a judge – active or retired – and four members, one representing landlords, one tenants and two representing the Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Social Affairs. The committee specifies the size of contributions depending on the income of the tenant and his household. If the average household income is not at least twice the minimum wage, the assistance of the fund covers the entire difference between the old and revised rental fees.

additional_laws.title_en: Judicial Organization Decree-Law No. 150/1983 (Draft Amending Law as submitted to the Venice Commission in 2022)
additional_laws.title_ar: المرسوم الاشتراعي رقم 150/1983 في تنظيم القضاء العدلي (مشروع القانون المُعدِّل المُقدَّم إلى لجنة البندقية عام 2022)
additional_laws.source: Venice Commission CDL-REF(2022)014 – Draft Law Amending Legislative Decree No. 150/1983
additional_laws.historical_context: Decree-Law No. 150 of September 16, 1983 governs the organization of Lebanon's ordinary courts (distinct from religious/personal status courts and the State Council for administrative courts). It establishes the structure of the court system, the composition and powers of the High Judicial Council (HJC), the appointment and discipline of judges, and related matters. The original decree has been criticized by international bodies including the ICJ and Venice Commission for allowing executive influence over judicial appointments and transfers. A draft law amending Decree-Law 150/83 was submitted to the Venice Commission in April 2022 and is reflected in the articles below.

articles.title: Role of Supreme Judicial Council
articles.content: The Supreme Judicial Council shall ensure the good conduct and independence of the judicial process and the proper functioning in courts and shall take the necessary decisions in this regard.

articles.title: Council Composition
articles.content: The Supreme Judicial Council shall be composed of ten members as follows: A- Statutory Members: First President of Court of Cassation ('President'); Attorney-General before Court of Cassation ('Vice-President'); President of Judicial Inspection Authority ('Member'). Such Statutory Members shall be appointed for four renewable years. B- Elected Members, who are: Accredited Judge as one of the Chamber Presidents in Court of Cassation; Accredited Judge as one of the Counsellors in Court of Cassation; Accredited Judge as one of the Chamber Presidents in Courts of Appeal; Accredited Judge as one of the Counsellors in Courts of Appeal; Accredited Judge as one of the Investigation Judges; Accredited Judge as one of the Chambers Presidents in Courts of First Instance; Accredited Judge as one of the Duty Judges and Sole Judges.

articles.title: Election of Members
articles.content: The electing authority composed of all judges shall meet in the Palace of Justice in Beirut on the calling date. The election shall be made by the secret ballot, and every judge shall elect two candidates from the declared candidates list; conditioned that a judge shall choose at least one candidate from his original category.

articles.title: Term of Office
articles.content: The nomination period of the elected members shall be three non-renewable years, except after passing a full period of their leaving the membership of the Supreme Judicial Council. The employment period of the Supreme Judicial Council members shall expire in case of death, resignation, and retirement or of issuance of a resolution related to applying a conduct penalty.

articles.title: Obligations of Members
articles.content: Neither member of the Supreme Judicial Council nor any of his relatives of Judges shall be transferred from one office to another till the second degree throughout his office period. A member may not, even after expiration of his office period, be candidate for the presidential, prosecution or municipal elections, nor be appointed as a minister or member in the constitutional council. The Bank Confidentiality of the Supreme Judicial Council members, their wives and minors shall be disclosed for the benefit of the National Authority for Combating Corruption and the Judicial Inspection Authority, immediately after the beginning of the Council's works.

articles.title: General Power of the Council
articles.content: The Council shall ensure the moral and material rights of judges, their fairness, and everything related to their independence, appointment, formation, transfer and discipline. The Council exercises this authority in accordance with the provisions of this law and other laws in force.

articles.title: Complaints
articles.content: Any person may file a complaint with the Supreme Judicial Council; provided that it is related to the functioning of the public service of justice, the conduct of the judge, or the independence of the judiciary. The complaint shall be in writing, signed, and shall contain the full name of the complainant, the date and a brief description of the facts.

articles.title: Council Meetings and Decisions
articles.content: The Council meets at the call of its president. The call requires convening the Council at least once a week. The sessions of the Council shall not be deemed to be legal unless two thirds of its members are present. Except for cases in which the law provides for a special majority, the decisions of the Council shall be taken by a majority vote of those present. In the event of equality, the vote of the chairman shall be deemed the casting vote. In all cases and regardless of the number of attending members, no decision is taken for the Supreme Council with less than five votes.

articles.title: Right of Appeal Against Council Decisions
articles.content: Individual and non-organizational decisions issued by the Council are subject to appeal before the General Assembly of the Court of Cassation. The review of the challenge shall be submitted according to the emergency procedures, within two weeks from the date of its notification to the person concerned. The review shall not suspend the implementation of the challenged decisions unless the General Authority of the Court of Cassation decides to suspend the execution.

articles.title: Court System Structure
articles.content: The Courts of Justice include: A- Courts of First Instance. B- Courts of Appeal. C- Court of Cassation. In addition to the specialized courts established by law, which consist of court judges or in which a court judge participates.

articles.title: Courts of First Instance
articles.content: Courts of the First Instance are composed of chambers that pass judgments on a president and two members. The number of courts of First Instance, their chambers and sections, the centres of these chambers and sections, and the scope of their spatial jurisdiction shall be specified in the relevant Table.

articles.title: Courts of Appeal
articles.content: Courts of Appeal are composed of chambers whose judgments are ruled by a president and two counsellors. Each Court of Appeal shall have a Public Prosecution presided by an Appellate Attorney-General assisted by one or more public attorneys, and an investigation department composed of a first investigative judge assisted by one or more investigative judges.

articles.title: Court of Cassation
articles.content: The Court of Cassation has a General authority composed of the presidents of Court Chambers. The Court of Cassation shall have a Public Prosecution presided by the Public Prosecutor at the Court of Cassation, assisted by Public Attorneys. Each chamber consists of a chairman and two counsellors exclusively.

articles.title: Headquarters of the Court of Cassation
articles.content: The headquarters of the Court of Cassation shall be in Beirut.

articles.title: First President of Court of Cassation
articles.content: First President, President of the Supreme Judicial Council, shall preside over the Court of Cassation and its general authority, and the Judicial Council in accordance with the provisions of Article (2) of this law, and he shall also preside over the Judicial Council.
